extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, physicians, surgeons, instrument-makers and natural historians (readers/members of the Royal Society)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and reporting natural-philosophy / medical / instrument-design accounts: how to record observations, present hypotheses, and specify experimental or instrument details for a learned audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold natural-history account
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be a threefold account given; a physiological, an anatomical, and a medical; and these taken rather from autopsy than books, and of our own country, rather than the whole world; and to begin from the lowest degree of animation in zoophytes, or plant-animals, so ascending by nature's clue, to run through all the several tribes of animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer firsthand dissection/autopsy evidence over secondhand book reports; start with the simplest organisms (zoophytes) and ascend taxonomically; treat physiological, anatomical and medical aspects separately so each is clearly documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study anomalous species as representative
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a good account of some of the most anomalous and heteroclite sorts of animals, or of those whose species are most different; for one of these may serve in a great measure for those of the whole genus, as the anatomy of a porpus for the cetaceous kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect detailed descriptions of unusual or extreme examples because a well-documented anomalous specimen can illuminate characteristics of an entire genus; emphasize careful anatomical comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present hypotheses modestly and support with demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: I endeavoured to prove ... and in that printed paper it was said, a muscle in contraction swelled like a bladder ... These and several other particulars I endeavoured to make out at large in those lectures; yet only in the way of an hypothesis, not as if I did presume to believe I had found out the true secret of animal motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame mechanistic accounts as hypotheses rather than definitive truths; accompany hypotheses with experiments, demonstrations, and responses to objections; avoid overclaiming.

rubrics_metrics.name: A good mechanistic theory must explain multiple observed phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory hypothesis should account for: the manner of the blood's circulation in each particular muscle; what the perspiration out of each muscle did towards it; that there was some swelling in the contraction of each muscle; how every muscle in contraction grows more hard, dense, and compact; the necessary cause of every muscle having its antagonist; why on a paralysis or wound of one side, the antagonist presently contracts; why upon fractures it runs up; why in animals killed, while the flesh is warm, there appear so many jerks and contractions of muscles; why a muscle cut in the middle runs up to each end, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing a theory of physiology/mechanics, enumerate and address the range of empirical phenomena it must explain; use experiments and figures to demonstrate how the theory accounts for those facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overinterpreting single chemical observations; use appropriate controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Little light is thrown upon the nature of contagion by this chemical observation. Pus taken from a common ulcer or abscess would doubtless yield, when urged by the fire, a product as fetid and as acrimonious as that obtained in the above recited experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attribute unique causal significance to a chemical product observed from a single source without comparing to relevant controls; acknowledge alternative sources and limitations of the experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical contagion-prevention recommendations for practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever converses with patients affected with any disease whatever, if he would preserve himself from infection, must be sure so long as he abides within the sphere of their steams never to swallow his spittle, but to spit it out. Strong smelling and strong tasting substances kept in the mouth, and chewed to promote spitting, are of very good and necessary use for physicians, surgeons, and apothecaries ... cleanse the nose as well as the mouth; wash the hands and face after visiting the sick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear, actionable precautions for clinicians visiting infected patients (avoid swallowing saliva, promote expectoration, use strong-tasting substances to encourage spitting, cleanse nose and mouth, wash hands and face). Footnotes caution that these measures are not singly sufficient and other routes (inhalation, skin pores) can transmit contagion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument/design superiority criteria (lamp example)
rubrics_metrics.description: This lamp is free from all the inconveniencies that Cardan's lamp is subject to. First, the air does not get into it by starts ... Secondly, when the air contained in the cavity AF comes to be rarefied by heat, it drives out much oil, and so may choke up Cardan's lamp; but in this the oil being so driven out, gets into the space between the two bottoms ... Thirdly, the oil being always kept nearly at the same distance from the flame, the wick will not be quickly consumed. Fourthly, you have the conveniency of putting new oil into the lamp without moving or extinguishing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing an improved device, list specific failure modes of prior designs and show how the new design addresses each (prevent sudden air ingress, avoid oil choking when air rarefies, maintain consistent oil-to-flame distance to slow wick consumption, allow refilling without extinguishing). Include schematic parts and explain functional roles of components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit assembly and operating procedure for instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: For filling up this machine, stop the aperture G of the pipe IG with a long pin fitted for that purpose, as also the upper end of the pipe LM; then pour in the oil by the aperture N; which done, the aperture N is to be shut up exactly, and both the others, G and L to be opened. ... When we fill the lamp, we must take care that the pipe L be well closed, so that the air between the two bottoms, finding no vent, may keep the oil from filling that space ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide step-by-step, reproducible instructions for filling, operating and maintaining instruments (which valves/pipes to close/open and in what order), and note critical cautions (e.g., close pipe L when filling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Calendar/almanac design principles
rubrics_metrics.description: This Al-mon-ac measures time principally by the moon, but with a great and near respect to the annual motion of the sun ... The new year and account may best begin with the vernal equinox; or rather with the day of the new moon happening near midnight about that time ... Once every century, or to one year in 100, add one day ... Which additional day being omitted every 230th or 240th century ... will balance the account for ever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing a calendar, state the primary astronomical unit (moon vs sun), justify the choice (observability, historical data), specify the month-length pattern and multi-year cycle (here a 38-year cycle), set rules for epoch/new-year choice (vernal equinox/new moon), and provide leap-day correction rules to maintain long-term alignment.
